hypotheses.justification:
The statement does not need `[Finite G]` to elaborate. `pi27` is defined as `qPi (W.subgroupOf (normalizer W))` and `qPi` never uses its `[Finite M]` variable, because `CFSG.oddCore` is `sSup {N | N.Normal ∧ Odd (Nat.card N)}`. The file already shows this: `pi27_surjective` and `qPi_surjective` are stated with `omit [Finite G] in` / `omit [Finite M] in`, and they mention `pi27 W` / `qPi K`. Lean removes omitted instance variables from the header context (`withHeaderSecVars`), so those statements would not elaborate if `pi27` or `qPi` needed `Finite`. So `pi27 W ⟨t, ht⟩ ≠ 1` is still well-formed after `omit [Finite G] in`.

The statement is still true for an arbitrary group `G`. Let `N = normalizer W` and `Q = N/W`. If `pi27 W ⟨t,ht⟩ = 1`, then the class `t̄ ∈ Q` lies in `oddCore Q`. That is the sup of the normal subgroups of odd `Nat.card`. A subgroup with odd `Nat.card` is finite, because `Nat.card` of an infinite type is 0, which is even. The set of such subgroups is directed: for normal `N₁, N₂` of odd order, `N₁ ⊔ N₂` has order `|N₁| · [N₂ : N₁ ⊓ N₂]`, which is odd. Hence every element of `oddCore Q` lies in a single finite odd-order normal subgroup, by `Subgroup.mem_sSup_of_directedOn`, and so has odd order. Since `t*t = 1`, we get `t̄² = 1`, so `t̄` has order dividing 2 and also odd order, so `t̄ = 1`. That means `t ∈ W`, contradicting `htW`.

The current proof uses `Finite G` only through `exists_odd_pow_mem_of_mem_ker_qPi` (it needs `[Finite M]`, supplied via `Finite ↥(normalizer W)`). To drop the hypothesis, replace that one step by a finite-free lemma: every element of `oddCore Q` has odd order. The rest of the argument, `hpow` and `mem_subgroupOf`, is unchanged. The other hypotheses `ht`, `ht2` and `htW` are all used.
